Working market model, with explicit assumptions. The range is not an independently confirmed market census.

Market size & growth

  • €7.6bn central installed-market estimate in 2025. The €4.1–14.8bn model range is driven by private volumes and installed costs; it is not a reported census.
  • Public charging stock expanded 20% in 2025. EAFO net additions were 56.7k DC and 123.2k AC points. Net additions do not measure replacement flows or private installations.
  • The base scenario grows installed spend 9.2% a year to 2030. This is an analyst trajectory; adoption, utilisation and delivery produce materially different downside and upside outcomes.
Explore →

Value pools

  • DC represents about 58% of central model spending. Power, civil works and connection costs make its spending weight larger than its share of public points.
  • Installed expenditure is wider than charger revenue. Equipment, installation and grid works share the buyer’s budget. Category spending shares are not supplier revenues or margins.
Explore →

Growth conditions

  • Vehicle demand creates opportunity; project conversion determines delivery. Grid access, site returns, charger reuse and utilisation affect the amount and timing of new investment.
  • Policy requirements need a project-level bridge. Coverage gaps and qualifying building works can create demand. Targets and pre-cabling cannot be counted as installed chargers.
Explore →

Competition & channels

  • Compare manufacturers, channel partners and integrators separately. Their offers address different parts of procurement; European product reach does not establish market-share leadership.
  • Win the party controlling the specification and order. Local distribution and installer access matter alongside equipment; complex sites also require integration and grid coordination.
Explore →

Expert perspectives

  • Collected expert views support grid and economics as decision variables. Some qualify the effect by site conditions and mitigation. These opinions do not directly validate the market-size or growth figures.
Explore →

Implications for a market participant

DC charging

Prioritise deliverable sites, grid capacity and utilisation. Hardware sales alone understate the installed project opportunity.

Residential AC

Win installation conversion and replacement demand. More electric vehicles need not mean one new home charger per vehicle.

Public & commercial AC

Target dwell-time use cases and building projects with a clear owner, budget and procurement route.

EAFO public charging stock

Independent investment-needs scenario

T&E’s €84.5bn light-duty requirement over 2025–2030 averages about €14.1bn/year. It exceeds the central 2025 estimate, as a cumulative transition scenario can. Compare deployment assumptions and private charging volumes before drawing conclusions; it cannot validate the base-year total.

Separate scenario methodology; infrastructure starting stocks can share EAFO ancestry. Not averaged into the headline.

Adoption creates demand; access, utilisation and grid delivery decide investment

DC charging

High installed costs give DC a large spending role. Grid access and site utilisation limit project delivery.

Residential AC

Residential volumes depend on vehicle adoption, parking access and charger reuse. Each vehicle does not require a new installation.

Public & commercial AC

Long dwell times support public and workplace AC. Property ownership, procurement and shared works decide which projects proceed.

Impact is an analyst judgment on 2025–2030 installed spending, separate from evidence confidence. Factors interact; their impacts are not additive.

Five strongest drivers and five strongest barriers

Each column has its own ranking. Items on the same row are not matched pairs or offsetting effects.

Growth driversInvestment barriers
1. Electric vehicle adoption High impact · Medium evidence

A larger active plug-in fleet increases energy demand; infrastructure response depends on existing capacity.

1. Grid and permitting delays High impact · Medium evidence

Connection and site delays move investment beyond the planned commissioning year.

2. Higher-power project mix High impact · Medium evidence

Higher power and tougher sites can raise installed cost per point.

2. Weak site economics High impact · Medium evidence

Low utilisation or high site costs can stop commercial projects despite growing EV demand.

3. Fleet and depot conversion High impact · Medium evidence

Fleet conversion can create complete depot projects, including grid and civil works.

3. Slower vehicle adoption High impact · Medium evidence

Slower adoption or lower electric mileage weakens the demand underpinning new projects.

4. Charging beyond the home High impact · Medium evidence

Drivers without home charging shift demand toward public and workplace facilities.

4. More use per charger High impact · Medium evidence

Higher throughput per point can absorb vehicle growth without proportional installation growth.

5. Residual AFIR investment Medium impact · Medium evidence

Coverage gaps can trigger projects even where aggregate national charging capacity is adequate.

5. Home access and ownership High impact · Medium evidence

Parking access, tenancy and shared-building decisions constrain home installation demand.

Light blue: verified profiles · Dark blue: contributing experts. Groups describe professional affiliation, not geographic representation.

The story across expert perspectives

Synthesis of the collected public statements, not commissioned interviews or a representative survey.

  • Demand must become an investable site. Alpitronic, IONITY, ING and RAP link rollout to utilisation, investment costs and commercial viability.
  • Grid access is a recurring constraint. Vehicle makers, operators, banks, logistics and network voices identify connection and permitting delays as obstacles to delivery.
  • Severity depends on the site. XCharge, RAP and public authorities describe how storage, flexible connections and smart charging can ease constraints.
  • Mitigation needs a business case. XCharge proposes storage where grid expansion is costly; that does not prove storage is economic at every site.
  • Home access redirects demand. Rabobank flags shared-property costs and landlord incentives; IONITY points to urban fast charging for drivers without home access.
  • The views test the growth mechanism. They inform delivery and utilisation scenarios, without directly endorsing the study’s market-size range or CAGR.

Where experts agree — and what that means for the model

Each row tests a specific proposition. Bars count organisations with direct evidence, not all screened people. Related views inform research but do not count as agreement.

What does conditional support mean?

The expert accepts the mechanism but limits when, where or how strongly it applies. Orange marks these explicit conditions; it does not mean weaker evidence or half a vote.

Evidence, context & model inputs

Annual DC points: 60,000 / 68,000 / 80,000 points/year (low / base / high).

EAFO public net increase = 56,698. Gross all-DC working bounds add roughly 3,300–23,300 points for replacements, private depots and coverage uncertainty. Central 68,000 adds 11,302. These increments are analyst allowances, not measured private installations; trucks already in public stock are not added again.

Annual residential AC points: 801,658 / 1,242,653 / 1,820,535 points/year (low / base / high).

2,896,257 BEV+PHEV registrations × eligible-home/parking fraction (45/60/70%) × new-install attach rate after reuse (50/60/75%), plus 150/200/300k replacement and used-car-triggered installations. Fractions and additions are explicit assumptions. The parking factor excludes non-residential installations; no one-charger-per-car claim.

Annual public & commercial AC points: 230,000 / 320,000 / 405,000 points/year (low / base / high).

Public AC net increase = 123,180. Add 100/180/250k private workplace/destination/fleet points and approximately 7/17/32k replacement/coverage allowance to form rounded 230/320/405k bounds. Private volume is assumed, not publicly counted; excludes residential points and all DC.

DC installed cost per point: 45,000 / 65,000 / 95,000 EUR/point (low / base / high).

Weighted installed-cost assumption across lower-power DC, passenger HPC and depot projects. Dutch station reference costs anchor order of magnitude; shared cabinets can reduce per-point hardware while site/grid work adds cost. Central €65k includes €35k equipment, €15k installation/civil and €15k allocated grid. Power/port mix is the main uncertainty; not a reported EU mean.

Residential installed cost per point: 1,000 / 1,500 / 2,500 EUR/point (low / base / high).

German gross €1,200–3,500 guidance corresponds to roughly €1,010–2,940 net at19% VAT. Use €1,000–2,500 for the 2025 EU mixture of new installs and cheaper replacements; central €1,500. Country, dwelling and later-source-year transfer are unmeasured assumptions, not an inflation adjustment.

Public & commercial AC installed cost: 2,500 / 4,000 / 6,500 EUR/point (low / base / high).

Dutch AC reference cost is €2,000 per ≥11kW station or €4,000 per dual station. Add assumed shared installation, civil works and grid allocation. Working installed range €2,500–6,500 per point spans ready sites and harder public/building projects; central €4,000. Not a supplier revenue or margin estimate.

How to read expert agreement

These are coded public statements, not responses to a representative survey. Agreement applies only to the stated proposition, not to the full forecast. Each named organisation contributes at most one position per row. Support and challenge within one organisation are mixed; explicit qualifications are conditional. Affiliation clusters do not imply absence of commercial interests or common source dependence.

Win the equipment order and the specification that drives it

The buyer controls the budget; its chosen procurement route determines who sells, specifies and installs the charging system.

Who controls the route to the customer?

Commercial role map based on the study’s documented routes. Roles can sit in the same company; this is not a mandatory four-transaction chain.

Equipment and installation delivered to the asset owner →
Equipment supplier

Manufacturers

Role in the chain

Builds charging equipment and supplies it directly or through a partner.

Decision influence

Product capability, compatibility and availability shape the shortlist.

Commercial priority

Win the technical specification and support the party placing the equipment order.

→
Supply & local installation

Distributors / Installers

Role in the chain

Distributors supply contractors; installers fit equipment and may sell the installed package.

Decision influence

Controls the offered range and quote when it is the invoicing seller.

Commercial priority

Secure channel access where the partner controls the offer; check who invoices whom.

→
System design & coordination

Integrators

Role in the chain

Coordinates equipment, site works, energy controls and commissioning across suppliers.

Decision influence

Site feasibility and installation requirements influence equipment selection.

Commercial priority

Make the product easy to specify, install and service; resolve grid and site constraints early.

→
Budget & asset ownership

Infrastructure buyer

Role in the chain

Household, property owner, fleet, public authority or infrastructure investor.

Decision influence

Approves the budget and procurement route. It may delegate product choice.

Commercial priority

Identify the budget holder and procurement criteria; the charging user may be a different party.

Challenges and opportunities by stage

Analyst implications from the role map, expert evidence and company offers. These are priorities to test, not measured company weaknesses.

Stage / examplesMain challengeCommercial opportunity
ManufacturersAlpitronic · ABB · Kempower · AlfenProduct differentiation and support must survive buyer scrutiny of installed cost.Combine fit-for-purpose hardware with service, interoperability and partner training.
Distributors / InstallersRexel · Sonepar · local electrical contractorsAvailability, quote conversion and local delivery capacity can constrain orders.Bundle equipment, accessories and commissioning; build installer competence.
IntegratorsSPIE · Equans · The Mobility House SolutionsGrid, civil works and multi-vendor interfaces create schedule and delivery risk.Win complex sites through design, controls and accountable commissioning.
Infrastructure buyersCPOs · fleets · property owners · householdsUncertain use and connection timing can undermine the investment case.Phase capacity to demand and secure the connection before committing full CAPEX.

Three ways the buyer reaches the supplier

Direct equipment purchase

Manufacturer or reseller → buyer

Buyer contracts installation and site works separately.

Win the buyer’s equipment decision and qualify with its installer.

Installed charging package

Manufacturer / reseller → installer or integrator → buyer

A package seller combines equipment and installation.

Win the package provider’s specification and offer; confirm who carries delivery risk.

Part of a building project

Equipment supply → electrical contractor → main contractor → buyer

Charging is included in a wider construction contract.

Engage the designer and electrical contractor before the building tender is fixed.

Translate the route into a sales priority

DC charging

Qualify with the asset owner and project integrator. Grid feasibility and commissioning can determine whether the order proceeds.

Residential AC

For supply-and-install offers, focus on the package seller and installer. For direct purchases, serve the household and its electrician.

Public & commercial AC

In building projects, reach the property buyer, designer and contractor early. In standalone projects, identify the buyer or integrator placing the order.

Analyst sales implications, not measured channel shares. Count installed asset expenditure once; operating receipts and financing flows are separate.

Evidence: Commission procurement guidance, section 4. Route-specific records and examples remain below.

Equipment, channel access and project delivery create different competitive advantages

Compare companies at the role they play in procurement, then test how their offer fits the charging use case.

Key competitive themes

ThemeFindingsCommercial implication
Compete within the right peer group
  • DC specialists, AC suppliers, distributors and integrators play different roles in the same project.
Alpitronic · Alfen · Rexel · SPIE		Compare like-for-like offers before comparing prices or revenue.
The site system matters alongside the charger
  • Load management, software and integration feature in manufacturer and specialist offers.
MENNEKES · Smappee · The Mobility House Solutions		Test equipment, energy controls and support together in procurement.
Channel access has a national layer
  • Large electrical distributors span the four priority countries through local businesses.
Rexel · Sonepar		Qualify national buying teams and installer networks, not just group headquarters.
Deployment growth does not guarantee supplier growth
  • Alfen reported weaker H1 2025 charging sales; Kempower grew 2025 revenue 12%. Periods and product mixes differ.
Alfen · Kempower		Test product mix, inventory and customer exposure before extrapolating growth.
Installed-market value extends beyond hardware
  • SPIE and Equans provide project services; Mobility House adds charging and energy management.
SPIE · Equans · The Mobility House Solutions		Separate equipment revenue from works, integration and operating income.

Right to win — and what to challenge

Capabilities are grounded in the linked company materials. Commercial readings and diligence questions are analyst judgments; company claims do not establish customer preference.

Company / stagePotential basis to winConstraint or diligence question
AlpitronicManufacturersBroad DC power range and an established deployed base.Compare service response and total installed cost at the required power.

Critical regulations: what changes the decision?

The commercial readings below are analyst implications. They do not quantify additional market spending.

High criticality

AFIR deployment

DC projects and connection works

Capacity and corridor requirements can create projects where provision is insufficient.

Map the compliance gap and secured grid capacity before converting targets into incremental spending.

Obligation, dates and sources

Alternative Fuels Infrastructure Regulation (AFIR), Regulation (EU) 2023/1804 of 13 September 2023: deployment

Analyst judgment: binding deployment requirements across EU27, with substantial obligations inside the forecast horizon and direct consequences for DC projects.

AFIR Article 3 requires each EU Member State, at each year-end from 2024, to provide publicly accessible charging power totalling at least 1.3 kW per registered light-duty BEV plus 0.80 kW per registered light-duty PHEV, subject to Commission-authorised relief under Article 3(2)–(3).

SINGLE_SOURCE governing legal instrument; official explanatory material is not independent legislation. This is a required capacity stock, not annual construction expenditure or proof of compliance. Count station power, avoiding double-counting shared-power connectors.

2023-10-12 · Law

Regulation (EU) 2023/1804 entered into force on 12 October 2023.

SINGLE_SOURCE legal family. Conflicting commentary does not overturn the explicit legal chronology.

2024-04-13 · Law

Article 26 of Regulation (EU) 2023/1804 sets 13 April 2024 as its general application date in EU Member States.

SINGLE_SOURCE legal family. General application does not make every infrastructure deadline fall on that date.

2024-12-31; annually thereafter · Law

AFIR Article 3(1) requires each EU Member State to meet its cumulative fleet-linked public charging power targets at each year-end beginning on 31 December 2024, subject to Article 3(2)–(3).

SINGLE_SOURCE legal family. This verifies the compliance schedule, not actual compliance by any Member State.

2025-12-31 · Law

Subject to Article 3 derogations, AFIR requires publicly accessible light-duty charging pools along the TEN-T core road network in each direction, at most 60 km apart, with at least 400 kW per pool and one point of at least 150 kW by 31 December 2025.

SINGLE_SOURCE legal family. Directional coverage does not necessarily require separate physical sites. Preserve the allowances and derogations in any capacity calculation.

2025-12-31 · Law

Subject to Article 4 allowances and derogations, AFIR requires publicly accessible heavy-duty charging pools in each direction along at least 15% of each Member State's TEN-T road-network length by 31 December 2025, with at least 1,400 kW per pool and one point of at least 350 kW.

SINGLE_SOURCE legal family. The legal claim holds, but the supplied measurement basis is not a complete executable coverage methodology. DG MOVE Questions 4.1, 4.11 and 4.19 must be considered before calculating required infrastructure.

2025-12-31 · Law

AFIR Article 4(1)(g) requires publicly accessible heavy-duty charging points aggregating at least 900 kW in each covered urban node by 31 December 2025, provided by stations individually offering at least 150 kW.

SINGLE_SOURCE legal family. Reject the slide's per-point interpretation. The requirement does not establish actual installed capacity, a mandatory single pool, or additional capacity separate from qualifying TEN-T infrastructure.

Deadline: 2026-12-31 · Law

AFIR Article 24(2) requires the European Commission to review the regulation by 31 December 2026.

SINGLE_SOURCE: one governing legal instrument. A review deadline does not establish completion or an amendment's commencement.

2027-12-31 · Law

Under AFIR Article 3(4)(a)(ii), by 31 December 2027 EU Member States must provide publicly accessible light-duty charging pools along the TEN-T core road network in each direction, no more than 60 kilometres apart, with at least 600 kW per pool and two points each providing at least 150 kW, subject to Article 3's shared-pool provisions and derogations.

SINGLE_SOURCE: statutory requirement only. Preserve the stated shared-pool and derogation qualifications in synthesis.

2027-12-31 · Law

Under AFIR Article 3(4)(b)(i), by 31 December 2027 each EU Member State must cover at least 50% of its TEN-T comprehensive road-network length with publicly accessible light-duty charging pools in each direction, no more than 60 kilometres apart, providing at least 300 kW per pool and one point of at least 150 kW, subject to Article 3's conditions and derogations.

SINGLE_SOURCE. Operationalise the denominator as the comprehensive network excluding core roads. Commission guidance also counts both directions in numerator and denominator. Do not credit core-road compliance against this target.

2027-12-31 · Law

Under AFIR Article 4(1)(b), by 31 December 2027 each EU Member State must cover at least 50% of its TEN-T road-network length with publicly accessible heavy-duty charging pools in each direction, with core-network pools providing at least 2,800 kW and two points of at least 350 kW each, and comprehensive-network pools providing at least 1,400 kW and one point of at least 350 kW, subject to Article 4's conditions and derogations.

SINGLE_SOURCE. The 50% threshold applies to combined core and comprehensive road length. It does not require 50% coverage of each separately. Commission guidance counts both directions and permits qualifying infrastructure to meet overlapping heavy-duty targets.

2027-12-31 · Law

AFIR Article 4(1)(e) requires EU Member States to ensure that, by 31 December 2027, each safe and secure parking area certified under Regulation (EU) 2022/1012 has at least two publicly accessible heavy-duty charging stations, each providing at least 100 kW.

SINGLE_SOURCE. Preserve the certification boundary and station-level unit. The requirement does not establish the number of qualifying parking areas.

2027-12-31 · Law

AFIR Article 15(1) requires each EU Member State to submit its first standalone national progress report on implementation of its national policy framework to the European Commission by 31 December 2027.

SINGLE_SOURCE. 'First' applies to this AFIR reporting obligation, not to all historical alternative-fuels reporting.

2030-12-31 · Law

Under AFIR Article 3(4)(b)(ii), by 31 December 2030 EU Member States must provide publicly accessible light-duty charging pools along the TEN-T comprehensive road network in each direction, no more than 60 kilometres apart, with at least 300 kW per pool and one point providing at least 150 kW, subject to Article 3's shared-pool provisions and derogations.

SINGLE_SOURCE legal evidence family. Commission guidance limits corridor targets to completed network sections. Preserve the stated sharing and derogation qualifications when using this requirement.

By 2030-12-31 · Law

AFIR Article 4(1)(c) requires publicly accessible heavy-duty charging pools on the EU27 TEN-T core road network by 31 December 2030, normally in each travel direction at intervals no greater than 60 kilometres, with at least 3,600 kW per pool and two points of at least 350 kW each, subject to Article 4's sharing provisions and derogations.

SINGLE_SOURCE legal evidence family. Low-traffic and Cyprus provisions qualify the headline. Commission guidance requires both traffic and economic-justification conditions for the relevant derogations.

By 2030-12-31 · Law

AFIR Article 4(1)(d) requires publicly accessible heavy-duty charging pools on the EU27 TEN-T comprehensive road network by 31 December 2030, normally in each travel direction at intervals no greater than 100 kilometres, with at least 1,500 kW per pool and one point of at least 350 kW, subject to Article 4's sharing provisions and derogations.

SINGLE_SOURCE legal evidence family. The exceptions remain material. Do not substitute the core-network spacing requirement for this comprehensive-network requirement.

By 2030-12-31 · Law

AFIR Article 4(1)(h) requires each urban node within its EU27 scope to have publicly accessible heavy-duty charging points providing at least 1,800 kW in aggregate by 31 December 2030, through stations individually providing at least 150 kW.

SINGLE_SOURCE legal evidence family. Commission guidance identifies the applicable urban nodes through Regulation (EU) 2024/1679. The packet does not enumerate that denominator. Qualifying infrastructure may also satisfy corridor targets.

By 2030-12-31 · Law

AFIR Article 4(1)(f) requires every EU27 safe and secure parking area certified under Regulation (EU) 2022/1012 to have at least four publicly accessible heavy-duty charging stations, each providing at least 100 kW, by 31 December 2030.

SINGLE_SOURCE legal evidence family. The denominator is certified parking areas. Stations and points must not be treated as interchangeable units.

By 2035-12-31 · Law

AFIR Article 3(4)(b)(iii) requires publicly accessible light-duty charging pools on the EU27 TEN-T comprehensive road network to provide at least 600 kW per pool, including two points of at least 150 kW each, by 31 December 2035, subject to Article 3's sharing provisions and derogations.

SINGLE_SOURCE legal evidence family. Commission guidance distinguishes aggregated station ratings from simultaneous delivery and contracted grid capacity. This requirement cannot directly establish grid investment.

High criticality

AFIR technical standards

Product selection and procurement

Standards change the requirements for specified new or renovated equipment.

Check product conformity and installation date before procurement; do not assume every existing charger needs replacement.

Obligation, dates and sources

Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) 2025/656 of 2 April 2025: AFIR technical standards

Analyst judgment: directly affects new procurement across public and private charging from 2027, including Residential AC.

Under Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) 2025/656, publicly accessible AC and DC charging points for light- and heavy-duty electric vehicles installed or renovated from 1 January 2027 that offer automatic authentication and authorisation, such as plug-and-charge, must comply with both EN ISO 15118-2:2016 and EN ISO 15118-20:2022.

SINGLE_SOURCE legal family. This establishes a legal obligation, not implementation readiness, certification availability or replacement expenditure. CharIN commentary cannot change the statutory deadline.

2025-07-08 · Law

Milestone — Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) 2025/656 of 2 April 2025: AFIR technical standards: 2025-07-08: Technical standards amendment enters into force. Recorded legal status: law. Subject to the instrument's scope, thresholds and exemptions.

SINGLE_SOURCE legal family. Entry into force does not make every equipment obligation immediately applicable. The date follows from Article 2 independently of the dual-standard claim.

2026-01-08 · Law

Article 2 of Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) 2025/656 establishes 8 January 2026 as its general application date in the EU27.

SINGLE_SOURCE legal family. General application does not override the separately dated Annex provisions. The date is not dependent on interpretation of the dual-standard obligation.

Installations or renovations from 2027-01-01 · Law

Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) 2025/656 requires publicly accessible AC and DC recharging points for light- and heavy-duty electric vehicles installed or renovated from 1 January 2027 to comply, for interoperability purposes, with at least EN ISO 15118-20:2022.

SINGLE_SOURCE legal evidence family. Verification establishes the enacted requirement, not technical readiness, compliance, replacement volumes or mandatory activation of every optional functionality.

High criticality

Buildings · EPBD

Residential and commercial property channels

Building works can bring charging into construction procurement.

Target qualifying projects and check national rules; ducting and pre-cabling do not equal installed charging points.

Obligation, dates and sources

Energy Performance of Buildings Directive (EPBD), Directive (EU) 2024/1275 of 24 April 2024

Analyst judgment: affects residential and commercial property channels across EU27 during 2026–2030, but national implementation and ducting alternatives limit charger conversion.

Article 14(4) of Directive (EU) 2024/1275 requires Member States to ensure at least one recharging point in new residential buildings with more than three car parking spaces where the car park is inside or physically adjacent to the building, subject to Article 14(5) exemptions.

SINGLE_SOURCE legal evidence family. Exemptions are conditional Member State options. National implementation and resulting charger demand remain unverified.

2024-05-28 · Law

The European Commission states that Directive (EU) 2024/1275 entered into force on 28 May 2024.

SINGLE_SOURCE legal lineage. Commission pages are not independent datasets. Entry into force does not establish national transposition or compliance.

2026-05-29; specified exception 2025-01-01 · Law

Article 35(1) of Directive (EU) 2024/1275 sets 29 May 2026 as the deadline for Member States to transpose Articles 1–3, 5–29 and 32 and Annexes I–III and V–X, except that Article 17(15) has a 1 January 2025 deadline.

SINGLE_SOURCE legal evidence family. No national transposition audit was performed.

2027-01-01 · Law

Article 14(2)(a) of Directive (EU) 2024/1275 requires Member States, by 1 January 2027, to ensure that non-residential buildings with more than 20 car parking spaces have at least one recharging point per ten spaces or ducting for at least 50% of spaces, subject to permitted postponement and exemptions.

SINGLE_SOURCE legal authority. Ducting satisfies the stated alternative; this is not a minimum installed-charger forecast.

2029-01-01 · Law

Article 14(2) of Directive (EU) 2024/1275 permits Member States to postpone its requirement until 1 January 2029 for non-residential buildings renovated during the two years before 28 May 2024 to meet national requirements established under Article 8(3) of Directive 2010/31/EU.

SINGLE_SOURCE legal authority. Permission is conditional, not an automatic extension for every building.

2033-01-01 · Law

Article 14(2) of Directive (EU) 2024/1275 requires Member States to ensure pre-cabling for at least 50% of car parking spaces by 1 January 2033 at non-residential buildings with more than 20 spaces owned or occupied by public bodies, subject to Article 14(5) exemptions.

SINGLE_SOURCE legal authority. Pre-cabling does not establish operational charging capacity.

High criticality

Cars & vans CO₂

Underlying vehicle demand

Vehicle compliance rules affect the timing of electrification.

Stress vehicle adoption separately from charger attachment and keep the current law distinct from proposed changes.

Obligation, dates and sources

Cars and vans CO₂ standards, Regulation (EU) 2019/631 of 17 April 2019, amended by Regulations 2023/851 and 2025/1214

Analyst judgment: affects the principal underlying demand base across all charging categories, with material timing flexibility before 2030.

Article 4(1a) of Regulation (EU) 2019/631, inserted by Regulation (EU) 2025/1214, requires manufacturers subject to its car or van emissions targets to meet their applicable target over 2025–2027 using annual emissions and targets weighted by their new registrations, with pool values used for years of pool membership.

SINGLE_SOURCE legal authority. The Commission explanation is derivative and does not independently corroborate manufacturer performance. Pool emissions and targets are substituted, while the weighting remains based on the manufacturer's registrations.

2020-01-01 · Law

Article 19 of Regulation (EU) 2019/631 sets 1 January 2020 as the date from which the regulation applies in the countries comprising the EU27.

SINGLE_SOURCE legal authority. The EU27 wording identifies included countries; it must not imply that the regulation's historical coverage excluded the UK. No statistical denominator applies.

Target step beginning 2025-01-01 · Law

Article 1(4) of Regulation (EU) 2019/631 sets EU fleet-wide CO2 targets for new passenger cars and new light commercial vehicles at 15% below their respective statutory 2021 targets from 1 January 2025.

SINGLE_SOURCE legal authority. This is a fleet target reduction, not a measured reduction, an EV sales quota, or a uniform manufacturer obligation.

2025-07-09 · Law

Regulation (EU) 2025/1214, introducing manufacturer CO₂ compliance averaging for calendar years 2025–2027, entered into force in the EU27 on 9 July 2025.

SINGLE_SOURCE: one underlying legal instrument, independently inspected through two official publishers. Commencement and the retrospective calendar-year coverage are different dates.

2027-12-31; endpoint of calendar years 2025–2027 · Law

The manufacturer CO₂ averaging window established by Regulation (EU) 2025/1214 for calendar years 2025–2027 ends on 31 December 2027.

SINGLE_SOURCE: the endpoint is a calendar inference from one legal instrument. It is not an assessment, payment or enforcement deadline.

2030-01-01 milestone; legal text consolidated on 2023-12-03 · Law

Article 1(5) of Regulation (EU) 2019/631, as consolidated on 3 December 2023, sets EU fleet-wide CO₂ targets from 1 January 2030 at reductions of 55% for new passenger cars and 50% for new light commercial vehicles relative to their respective statutory 2021 targets.

SINGLE_SOURCE: official explanations derive from the same legislation. HOLDS for the specified historical consolidation; do not silently recast it as a complete current-policy assessment. A later proposal seeks to change the van target.

2035-01-01 milestone as established by the 2023 amendment · Law

Regulation (EU) 2023/851 established EU fleet-wide CO₂ targets from 1 January 2035 equal to a 100% reduction of the respective statutory 2021 targets for new passenger cars and new light commercial vehicles.

SINGLE_SOURCE: one enacted legal basis. Historical establishment is verified; certainty about the eventual 2035 regime or charging demand is not. Preserve the supplied current-status limitation.

High criticality

Vehicle CO₂ proposal

Scenario risk across all categories

A proposal can change investment expectations before becoming law.

Treat proposed changes as a scenario trigger; do not substitute them for enacted requirements.

Obligation, dates and sources

Commission proposal COM(2025)995 of 16 December 2025 amending cars and vans CO₂ standards

Analyst judgment: proposed changes touch the vehicle-demand foundation and the 2030 investment window, despite having no present legal force.

Commission proposal COM(2025)995 of 16 December 2025 amending cars and vans CO₂ standards: No current obligation. The proposal includes reducing the 2030 van target from 50% to 40%, averaging compliance over 2030–2032, and a 90% tailpipe reduction target from 2035 with specified compensating credits. It also proposes incentives for small electric cars made in the EU.

SINGLE_SOURCE proposal family, with separate institutional status inspection. Full EUR-Lex proposal text was blocked; the verdict covers the stated headline provisions supported by the accessible official descriptions, not an article-by-article legal audit. Banking and borrowing must not be implemented as an assumed unweighted arithmetic average. Status checked on 17 September 2026.

2025-12-16 · Proposal

Milestone — Commission proposal COM(2025)995 of 16 December 2025 amending cars and vans CO₂ standards: 2025-12-16: Commission proposes revised vehicle CO₂ rules. Recorded legal status: proposal. Subject to the instrument's scope, thresholds and exemptions.

SINGLE_SOURCE legislative-event family. The event is proposal publication, not entry into force. Procedural status is supported as inspected on 17 September 2026; substantive scope remains that of the proposed instrument.

2030-2032 · Proposal

Milestone — Commission proposal COM(2025)995 of 16 December 2025 amending cars and vans CO₂ standards: 2030-2032: Proposed compliance averaging window. Recorded legal status: proposal. Subject to the instrument's scope, thresholds and exemptions.

SINGLE_SOURCE legislative family. The Senate hosts the Commission document; it is not independent substantive evidence. Averaging concerns manufacturer compliance for new vehicles, not charging infrastructure deployment.

2035 · Proposal

Milestone — Commission proposal COM(2025)995 of 16 December 2025 amending cars and vans CO₂ standards: 2035: Proposed revised tailpipe target and compensating credits. Recorded legal status: proposal. Subject to the instrument's scope, thresholds and exemptions.

SINGLE_SOURCE legislative family. This is a proposed change to new-vehicle fleet emissions standards, not an adopted relaxation or a charging infrastructure requirement.

High criticality

Heavy-duty CO₂

Fleet and depot DC projects

Truck electrification can change project power and site requirements.

Test fleet replacement schedules against depot readiness; verify unresolved deadlines before phasing investment.

Obligation, dates and sources

Heavy-duty vehicle CO₂ standards, Regulation (EU) 2019/1242, amended by Regulations 2024/1610 and 2026/1046

Analyst judgment: can materially change DC project power, grid requirements and commissioning schedules through 2030.

Regulation (EU) 2026/1046 changes heavy-duty vehicle emission-credit calculations for reporting years 2025–2029 without changing the CO₂ reduction target levels established under Regulation (EU) 2019/1242.

SINGLE_SOURCE: one amending instrument. Unchanged numerical targets do not mean unchanged compliance stringency. Also distinguish the instrument's date, 29 April 2026, from the Council adoption decision on 30 March 2026.

Milestone dates need source reconciliation before they can be plotted.

High criticality

Electricity & grid access

Commissioning and grid design

Connection arrangements affect whether and when demand becomes an installed asset.

Check national connection conditions and flexible-connection options before fixing the delivery schedule.

Obligation, dates and sources

Electricity Directive (EU) 2019/944 of 5 June 2019, amended by Directive (EU) 2024/1711

Analyst judgment: grid access can determine whether investment is commissioned inside the forecast horizon, especially for DC charging.

Electricity Directive (EU) 2019/944 of 5 June 2019, amended by Directive (EU) 2024/1711: Article 33 requires a framework facilitating connections for public and private smart and bidirectional charging, and non-discriminatory distribution-operator cooperation. Distribution operators generally cannot own or operate charging points except own-use facilities or regulated derogations.

SINGLE_SOURCE legislative lineage. The charging amendment's transposition deadline was 17 January 2025. This verifies EU requirements, not implementation in every Member State or guaranteed grid access. Own use means private points solely for the operator's use; derogations have conditions.

2019 · Law

Macro sensitivity model (4)
Copper, aluminium and steel-related inputs
Copper, aluminium and steel-related inputs: SINGLE-SOURCE observations: August 2026 copper averaged USD 14,326 per metric tonne versus USD 9,947 for calendar 2025, a calculated increase of 44.0%; aluminium was USD 3,251 versus USD 2,632, up 23.5%.
Context and evidence

These are August-to-prior-calendar-average comparisons, not year-on-year growth. HYPOTHESIS: exposed equipment and cable costs rise with purchased metal prices, subject to contracts, inventories and hedging. Steel exposure remains unquantified; iron ore is not a finished-steel price. SINGLE_SOURCE World Bank benchmark observations. Underlying price collection was not independently replicated. These are dollar-denominated commodity comparisons, not euro-denominated charger-price inflation or quantified annual installed CAPEX effects.

Installation labour and civil-works inflation
Installation labour and civil-works inflation: SINGLE-SOURCE observation: EU construction hourly labour costs increased 3.9% year-on-year in the second quarter of 2026.
Context and evidence

HYPOTHESIS: installation and civil-works prices face wage pressure. This index cannot be applied to all installed CAPEX: labour shares, productivity, contractor margins and national project mix are unknown. Electrical-contractor capacity constraints were not quantified. SINGLE_SOURCE. No independent measurement corroborated the aggregate. The index measures nominal, calendar-adjusted hourly employer costs, including non-wage costs. It can change with workforce composition and hours worked. The release flags missing Belgian observations and possible revisions. It establishes neither electrical-contractor shortages nor a charging installation-price increase.

Electricity prices and charging utilisation
Electricity prices and charging utilisation: SINGLE-SOURCE observation: Eurostat reports EU non-household electricity at EUR 18.37 per 100 kWh in the second half of 2025 for the 500–2,000 MWh annual-consumption band.
Context and evidence

HYPOTHESIS: electricity costs affect charging margins and EV operating economics, influencing deployment indirectly. Country, consumption-band, tariff and tax differences prevent treating this as a universal charging procurement price. Electricity sales and operating purchases remain outside market CAPEX. SINGLE_SOURCE. EUR 18.37 per 100 kWh includes non-recoverable taxes and levies, alongside energy, supply and network costs. It is not an all-tax-excluded commodity price. No independent dataset or charging-specific procurement sample corroborated its applicability to operators. Neither charging utilisation nor deployment sensitivity is measured.

Economic growth, inflation and discretionary investment
Economic growth, inflation and discretionary investment: SINGLE-SOURCE forecast: the ECB's September 2026 baseline projects euro-area real GDP growth of 0.9% in 2026, 1.4% in 2027 and 1.5% in 2028, with headline inflation of 3.0%, 2.5% and 2.1%.
Context and evidence

HYPOTHESIS: weak growth can restrain vehicle purchases and discretionary property or fleet investment, while inflation can increase nominal installed expenditure without equivalent deployment growth. These projections do not cover all EU27 or extend to 2030. SINGLE_SOURCE. Both ECB documents belong to one forecast family. Verification establishes what the ECB projected, not whether those outcomes will occur. Headline HICP is not a charging-equipment or installation-cost deflator. The prose correctly limits geography to the euro area; the packet's EU27 metadata does not describe the forecast's actual coverage.

Research still worth doing

  • Private and replacement installation volumes are model assumptions. Collect national installation/grant records and supplier unit shipments to narrow them.
  • Installed unit-cost bounds use country references and site reasoning; obtain a power-stratified project sample with explicit ports, VAT and grid allocations.
  • A second independently scoped 2025 installed-spend pathway has not been reconciled. The headline remains a working estimate, not a confirmed market total.
  • Scenario growth rates are analyst stress assumptions. They need testing against adoption, utilisation, access and country-level delivery data.
  • Public expert evidence is strongest on grid and utilisation; independent coverage of private volumes, unit costs and regulatory additionality remains limited.

Financing expense is outside installed CAPEX.

Full Market Analyst workflow

The implemented execution sequence, including deterministic controls and optional stages. Arrows show processing order; this diagram is not a claim that every stage has completed for the current draft.

AgentCodeGateOptional
All workflow steps as text
  1. Approved study scope: Freeze geography, period, measurement basis, exclusions and decision.
  2. Lead planner: Assign questions, sources and deliverables. Failed plan gate stops research.
  3. Deterministic data pack: Retrieve mapped APIs and datasets; preserve units, periods and provenance.
  4. Value-chain agent: Map buyers, suppliers, channels, procurement and installed-cost boundaries.
  5. Regulation & macro agent: Identify obligations, milestones, criticality and commercial mechanisms.
  6. Demand agent: Build the full driver/barrier inventory and demand equations by category.
  7. Market-size agent: Develop independent sizing pathways; reconcile scope and assumptions.
  8. Industry-structure agent: Separate categories, value pools, supplier revenues and margins.
  9. Participants agent: Map competitors against comparable segments and denominators.
  10. Competitive intelligence: Optional price and seller research when enabled in the run.
  11. Evidence graph & source reads: Create claim IDs, revisions, dependencies and contradiction clusters; enrich sources.
  12. Independent claim verifier: Test source entailment, scope and contradictions for material claims.
  13. Targeted claim repair: Research failed claims; re-read sources and reverify changed claims once.
  14. Impact reassessment: Reassess drivers/barriers after repair. Impact and evidence confidence stay separate.
  15. Analytical model recovery: Charging workflow: research, calculate, independent challenge; at most two repair cycles.
  16. Expert-evidence panel: Scout stakeholder strata, verify identities and statements, deduplicate and assess claim positions.
  17. Quotation & dissent selection: Select contextual support and challenge from the verified expert registry.
  18. Synthesis agent: Write the consulting story using governed claims, caveats and eligible model outputs.
  19. Calculations & story architecture: Check arithmetic; assemble answer, proof, visual and implication; route missing evidence.
  20. Final editorial review: One bounded semantic review of the rendered content against its evidence.
  21. Publication gate: Check completeness, contradictions, evidence freshness, expert coverage and editorial approval.
  22. Save candidate / release decision: Keep incomplete work as a draft. Promotion and public export require their applicable gates.

Research and repair loops

Claim repair

Failed material claim → targeted research → source enrichment → independent reverification

One repair/reverification round in the main pipeline. Supported claims remain available; unresolved claims retain their actual status.

Numerical model

Research inputs → calculate → independent model challenge → targeted repair

Initial attempt plus at most two repair cycles. Scope is frozen. Exhaustion escalates the unresolved model; it does not manufacture agreement.

Expert coverage

Stakeholder scouts → deduplication → batched verification → coverage check → targeted refill

A bounded refill targets missing coverage. Opinion cannot verify historical market size; reused public statements cannot endorse a new assumption.

Story and usability

Evidence → finding → visual → decision implication → editorial review

A missing decision implication is routed to its owner for research or redesign. The editor cannot invent facts or automatically restart research.

Controls across the whole run

Checkpoints preserve completed work after each stage. Cancellation and cost limits are checked between stages. Targeted refresh invalidates dependent outputs. Changed claims and model packets invalidate stale approvals. Browser closure does not stop a live server-side run; stopping the server still interrupts it.

Current draft: the numerical recovery packet still requires independent model approval. This interface update used saved evidence and did not rerun the external research agents.

Source of truth: pipeline.py, recovery.py, expert_panel.py, refresh.py, editorial.py, publication.py and runner.py. Checked 21 September 2026.

Methodology & how to read this

How this study is built, and what the confidence labels mean.

Confidence
CONFIRMED — reported research tier; current independent support is recorded in the source audit
RESEARCHED — backed by one cited source
HYPOTHESIS — a qualitative assumption, scenario or unresolved input; not a verified fact
CONFLICTING — evidence remains unreconciled; no defensible range is implied
SINGLE_SOURCE — one underlying evidence family; multiple URLs are not independent corroboration
Audit verdicts
HOLDS — a supporting verdict; current usability also requires scope, revision and dependency checks
OVERSTATED — right direction, magnitude too strong
REFUTED — contradicted by what was found
UNCERTAIN — could not be independently confirmed
Source quality
Authoritative — official statistics, regulators, standards bodies, research institutes
Reputable — established press and major industry research
Other — vendor, trade or unattributed — read with care

The pipeline

The market is researched as a fixed sequence of specialist stages, each building on prior working research. Verification then determines which scoped claims can enter the narrative; unresolved estimates stay explicitly unestablished.

1
Lead Plan. the approved boundary, declared evidence needs and confirmation criteria.
2
Data Pack. the mapped deterministic APIs and source-traced series retrieved before agent analysis.
3
Value Chain. the routes to market (channels) and the price build-up from end-user price back to manufacturer price, where comparable observations support the steps.
4
Regulatory & Macro. enacted rules, proposals and timing before policy-dependent demand and scenarios.
5
Demand. the end-user demand equation, the growth drivers vs barriers, and what would have to be true for each.
6
Market Size. aim for at least two independent sizing pathways on one declared basis; show a reconciled range only when the evidence supports it.
7
Industry Structure & Value Pools. submarkets, component economics and category shares reconciled against the defined market denominator.
8
Participants. who plays at each value-chain stage, their share of the sized market, and concentration.
9
Verification. an adversarial audit that tries to refute the decision-critical claims.
10
Evidence Repair. one bounded attempt to narrow, support or retract failed material claims, followed by re-verification.
11
Expert Panel. named people, roles, affiliations and public statements checked separately. Study-specific coverage thresholds are shown in Expert Perspectives; identity counts do not validate claims.
12
Quotation Selection. on-point supporting and challenging voices selected only from the verified panel, followed by exact-source reopening.
13
Synthesis. the executive read — written only from eligible claim revisions; panel opinion remains interpretive context.
14
Final Story Review. a bounded review of the composed report against its evidence; publishing requires current approval and artifact integrity.

Key terms

Manufacturer price
The manufacturer's selling price at its own premises — before transport, downstream margins and VAT. Use only when the approved market boundary is manufacturer revenue.
End-user / installed spend
Spending at the final buyer boundary. Hardware, installation, civil works, grid works and tax treatment must match the declared study scope; there is no universal conversion multiple.
Consumer↔manufacturer ratio
The multiple between end-user price and manufacturer price for a channel — used to move a market size between the two bases without distorting it.
Channel
A distinct route a product takes to its buyer (e.g. OEM first-fit vs aftermarket). Price builds up differently per channel, so they are never blended.
Triangulation
Sizing a market by ≥2 independent methods and reconciling them; agreement raises confidence, divergence is itself a finding.
TAM / SAM / SOM
Total / Serviceable / Obtainable market — the whole market, the slice a player can address, and the slice it can realistically win.
Concentration (CR4 / HHI)
How consolidated a market is — CR4 = combined share of the top 4 players; HHI = sum of squared shares.
